name: Cassiodorus
knownFor: A Roman statesman in the service of the Gothic kings of Italy who wrote their letters, then founded the monastery of Vivarium and wrote for its monks a guide to sacred and secular reading.
dates: Consul in the year Theodor Mommsen numbers 514, by his own chronicle; praetorian prefect from the year Thomas Hodgkin gives as 533. He wrote on spelling in his ninety-third year, by his own word. Hodgkin, following Trithemius, puts his birth about 480 and his death in 575
place: Italy, at the Gothic court in Ravenna and at Rome; later Vivarium, near Scyllacium (Squillace) in the far south, where Hodgkin says his family came from
tradition: The Roman Church in the Age of Gregory the Great
role: Statesman; founder of the monastery of Vivarium; writer

keyWorks.title: Variae
keyWorks.about: twelve books of the letters he wrote for the Gothic kings and, as prefect, in his own name

keyWorks.title: Institutions of Divine and Secular Learning (Institutiones)
keyWorks.about: a guide for the monks of Vivarium to the reading of Scripture and its commentators, and to the liberal arts

keyWorks.title: Exposition of the Psalms (Expositio Psalmorum)
keyWorks.about: a commentary on the Psalms, which by his own word he began at the time of his turn to the religious life

traces: At Vivarium he set his monks to copy and bind books, and gave them self-trimming lamps, sundials and water-clocks for the work, as he describes in the Institutions.
With Pope Agapetus he planned a Christian school at Rome on the models of Alexandria and Nisibis; war stopped it, he says.
Jordanes says he condensed the twelve books of the Senator's History of the Goths, which is lost, into his own short work.
remembered: Hodgkin calls him "a statesman of considerable sagacity and of unblemished honour, a well-read scholar, and a devout Christian; but he was apt to crouch before the possessors of power however unworthy".
Alcuin of York lists Cassiodorus among the authors in the library of York.

uncertain: His years. No early source gives his birth or death. Hodgkin's 480 and 575 rest on Trithemius, a writer who died in 1516, whom Hodgkin calls "a very late and somewhat unsatisfactory source". Hugh Williams gives his death as 570. The one fixed point is his own "ninety-third year", which no source dates.
His name. Mommsen and Hodgkin hold that Senator was his own name, not a title. Paul the Deacon, two centuries later, took it as a rank.

Whether he was abbot or a Benedictine. He names two abbots, Chalcedonius and Gerontius, in the Institutions. Hodgkin thinks he never formally held the office, against Trithemius, and finds no mention of Benedict in his writings. Garet's argument on his monastic life is not held.
His History of the Goths is lost. Jordanes says he condensed it after a three days' reading, which Hodgkin calls false.
Much of his life is told in his own letters, some written in the king's name in praise of himself, as Hodgkin notes.
Hodgkin's English of the Variae is condensed. Most letters are summaries; the preface to Book I and the letter on Scyllacium are given in full.
